title: Imagine everyone can build their own automated trading bot/system—let's talk about it
author: Pupsi42069
selftext:
How long can this go on? Institutional investors have been using algorithms for years, on a scale that moves the markets. Now there are X new players entering the fray who analyze the market just as “well” and place their bets based on sophisticated algorithms. Where is this headed?

Not everyone can have a piece of the pie. There have to be some who don’t get a piece—it can’t be any other way. One person’s gain is another’s loss.

Let’s say: We have about 5 years left (though it feels like much less) during which a manageable, small number of new traders will use an AI to create a profitable trading system. After that, an even larger number of traders will enter the market—because getting started will be even easier. 

Today, after reading this thread, we know that developing such a system is still a bit tricky, especially if you’re not an expert—much like the difference between programming and Vibe Coding. 

But it's only a matter of time before this problem is solved.

What then?  
How do you think the (trading) market will react to these new circumstances?  
What adjustments will be made?

  
/Transparency  
This text was NOT generated by AI. I wrote it in my native language and had it translated using Deepl. That explains the generic style.

comments.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
comments.body:
I think the premise has a hole in it, and it's the part where AI makes profitable systems easy to build.

Building the system was never the hard bit. I had a working bot — 9,000 lines, walk-forward validation, the lot — and it lost money. Not because the code was bad. Because there was nothing in the signal. I spent far more effort finding that out than I did building the thing.

What AI is genuinely good at is producing a strategy that looks plausible and backtests well. That's the easy half, and it was already easy before. What it doesn't do is tell you whether the backtest means anything, and that's where almost everyone loses. I ran a random walk — pure noise, no predictability by construction — through a standard EMA feature and got a correlation of −0.30 with future returns at long horizons. Anyone who builds a system on top of that gets a beautiful equity curve from data that contains nothing.

So what I'd actually expect from cheaper system-building isn't a wave of profitable traders. It's a much larger wave of people who are confidently wrong, arriving faster, and paying fees the whole way down. The market's "adjustment" to that is the same as it's always been: it takes their money. That's not a new equilibrium, it's the existing one running at higher throughput.

There's a second reason the five-year clock probably doesn't tick the way you're describing. Edges don't survive being widely known — the moment a mechanism is discovered and shared, the capital that can exploit it arrives and compresses it. That's not a future risk from AI, it's the mechanism that has always kept this hard. AI speeds up discovery, which means it also speeds up decay. Both sides of that accelerate together.

Where I'd agree with you: the gap between retail and institutional is real and it isn't about who can write code. It's data and execution. Firms spend nine figures a year on datasets nobody outside can buy, and they trade at costs a retail account can't reach. I measured my own round-trip cost at 0.16% in crypto against a measured effect of 0.09%. No amount of better strategy generation closes a gap like that, because the gap isn't in the strategy.

The thing that would actually change the picture isn't AI writing better strategies. It's AI being honest about how little a given backtest proves — and that's a harder problem, because it's not what anyone wants from it.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
Your last point is the part I find most interesting.

Suppose you do the validation properly and eventually decide an effect is strong enough to trade. Once it's live, how do you decide later that the evidence supporting it has deteriorated?

Do you explicitly define things like expected effect size, cost assumptions, regime characteristics, correlations, volatility, etc., and monitor those prospectively — or is it mostly periodic re-validation / P&L deterioration?

I'm curious because AI making strategy generation cheaper seems like it could make *ongoing falsification* the harder problem, not just initial validation.

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
Good question — and honestly one of the more important ones.  
Once you’ve done proper validation and decided an effect is strong enough to trade, the real problem becomes: how do you know later that the evidence has deteriorated?  
I would handle it like this:  
1.  Pre-define the expected characteristics before going live:  
	•  expected effect size  
	•  cost assumptions  
	•  regimes / volatility / correlation conditions under which it should work  
	•  minimum statistical strength you still want to see on a rolling window  
2.  Monitor those characteristics directly, not just P&L:  
	•  rolling effect size and t-stat on recent independent observations  
	•  actual round-trip costs vs the ones you assumed  
	•  performance across different regimes  
	•  any structural changes in correlations or volatility  
P&L is a lagging and noisy signal. An edge can already be decaying while the equity curve still looks acceptable for a while (especially with some luck or a volatility shift).  
3.  Define kill criteria in advance. For example:  
	•  if the rolling estimate of the edge falls below X% of costs for Y days/trades → stop  
	•  or if the out-of-sample t-stat stays below a pre-set threshold  
Without that, it’s very easy to start rationalizing (“just a bad regime”, “need to tweak parameters a bit”, etc.).  
On the AI point: yes. Making strategy generation cheaper shifts the hard problem from initial validation to ongoing falsification. The easier it is to generate new ideas, the more important it becomes to have a strict, pre-committed process for killing them when they stop working. Otherwise you just keep hopping from one half-dead edge to the next.  
So I’d rather monitor the underlying characteristics of the signal explicitly than wait for the P&L to tell me something is wrong.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
That makes sense. 

Do you already have the rolling effect size, cost assumptions, regime conditions, kill criteria, etc. running automatically somewhere, or is it a mix of scripts / notebooks / dashboards that you revisit periodically?

I’m trying to understand whether ongoing falsification is mainly a discipline problem — defining the right criteria in advance — or also an infrastructure problem once you’re running multiple strategies.

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
Right now it’s still mostly discipline + scripts.  
I have a set of check scripts for effect size, costs, regimes, etc., but I run them manually or on a schedule when I’m actively evaluating something. There isn’t a full always-on monitoring layer that automatically flags kill criteria across multiple live strategies — because I don’t have multiple live strategies.  
The infrastructure problem only really appears once you have several things running in production at the same time. Until then, the bottleneck is still forcing yourself to pre-define the kill rules and actually respect them when the numbers start looking uncomfortable.  
So for me it’s currently 80% discipline, 20% light automation. The heavy infrastructure would come later, if anything survives long enough to need it.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body: That makes sense. I should be transparent about why I’m asking: I’m building an early system where a trader and their AI can take one hypothesis, formalize its assumptions and failure criteria, evaluate it using reproducible research instruments, and—if it survives—keep those same checks running prospectively. It can start with one candidate strategy; it doesn’t require several live ones. Would you be open to trying it with an idea you’re already exploring and telling me where it falls short?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
Appreciate the pitch. I'm pretty set on my current stack because I prefer full local control over my spec hashes and verification scripts (no black boxes or external pipelines).  
Out of curiosity though: how are you handling the historic execution cost matrix problem (fee/slippage drift over time) inside your framework, and is the evaluation executed entirely client-side/locally?

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
Fair questions. The honest answer is that the current beta doesn’t solve the historical execution-cost matrix end to end. Costs can be stated as explicit assumptions, but we don’t yet provide reliable venue-, order-type-, size- and liquidity-specific fee/slippage histories. We also wouldn’t infer those from candle data.

And no—the evaluation isn’t entirely client-side. Research and monitoring run inside ASNOMIC’s private server-side runtime. We preserve immutable experiment definitions, provenance and evidence history, but it isn’t a local-first system where you execute every verification script yourself.

So given your preference for complete local control, the current beta probably wouldn’t replace your stack. That’s a useful boundary for me to hear.

Completely understood on keeping execution and raw tick data local. That’s a clear boundary, and I won’t try to talk you out of it. Thanks for the thoughtful exchange, and good luck with the research.

Building the bot is the easy part now. You can vibecode a working strategy + execution layer in a weekend with current tools.  
The hard part is everything after that: making sure the edge is real, measuring costs honestly, surviving the overlap and multiple-testing corrections, and then deciding in live conditions when the thing has actually died instead of just having a bad week.  
Most people still think the bottleneck is “writing the code.” It’s not. The bottleneck is the part where you have to be willing to kill your own ideas.

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
You’re attempting to solve a fundamental trading problem by increasing architectural complexity rather than finding a real market edge. In software engineering, that’s classic over-engineering—and in algorithmic trading, it almost always leads to burning money faster.  
The multi-agent concept sounds great on paper, but it hits a hard wall when it meets real market microstructures:  
 **Latency Bottleneck:** If these agents rely on LLMs, a reasoning loop ("Agent A analyzes -> Agent B counter-argues -> System executes") takes anywhere from 3 to 15 seconds. By the time your agents reach a consensus, institutional algos have already stripped all the alpha out of the move.  
 **Amplifying Noise:** If not a single individual agent possesses a statistically proven, positive expected value (E\[X\] > 0), pooling 20 "blind" agents together won't yield collective intelligence. It just yields an averaged-out combination of noise, curve-fitted bias, and LLM hallucinations.  
 **Cost Structure Failure:** Running continuous, real-time API calls across dozens of agents will drain your capital on cloud infrastructure and token usage long before you cover execution costs.  
Multi-agent environments do exist in institutional quant funds, but they look entirely different. They aren't conversational LLMs debating market sentiment; they are isolated, deterministic mathematical models (e.g., one measuring statistical cointegration, one computing Order Flow Imbalance, and another dynamically enforcing VaR risk limits).  
If you want to build a system that actually survives live trading, strip away the complexity: find **one** verifiable market anomaly, prove its edge on out-of-sample data without lookahead bias, and account for spread and slippage before you write a single orchestration layer

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Your programming versus vibe coding comparison is the right one, but it cuts the other way too. Vibe coding got cheap and the amount of shipped broken software went up, not down.

Same here. Generating a strategy is already close to free. Deciding whether it actually works is not, and that second half is not getting easier at the same rate. So the flood probably does not arrive as thousands of systems that work, it arrives as thousands of overfit ones that looked fine until fees and fills showed up.

What makes you think the validation side gets solved on the same timeline as the generation side?

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
I think this distinction between generation and validation is probably the key one.

I'm also wondering whether there is a third stage after validation: once something has passed whatever standard you trust and goes live, how do you continuously test whether the assumptions behind that validation are still holding?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
There's a third stage and almost nobody builds it. The assumption that goes stale first isn't the edge, it's the fill.

We compare every live fill against the price the backtest assumed for that same trade. When that gap starts drifting, the validation is out of date before the signal is.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
That's interesting — comparing the actual fill against the price assumed by the backtest is a very clean test.

Is that something you've built as a persistent live check for every strategy, or do you review the drift periodically?

And when that fill gap deteriorates, do you already have a predefined threshold that disables/revalidates the strategy, or does a human make that judgment?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Per fill, every time, not a periodic review. Otherwise you find out weeks later and can't tell which day the drift started.

The threshold flags it, a person decides. Auto-disable sounds clean until one wide day pulls a strategy that was fine. Where would you put that line?

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
That sounds like the right balance to me. One unusually wide day shouldn’t automatically kill a strategy, so having the threshold raise a flag and a person interpret the context makes sense.

I’d put the line where the fill deterioration persists long enough to materially change the strategy’s expected economics, rather than at any single bad fill or day.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Normalising it against the strategy's own average edge per trade is what makes that line portable. The same few cents of drift is noise on a multi-day hold and fatal on something scalping a tick or two, so one fixed slippage number means different things per strategy.

Do you track the drift in absolute terms, or as a share of expected edge?

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
That makes sense—the share of expected edge gives the absolute number context.

I should clarify that my earlier answer was a design thought. I’m building a tool for monitoring trading theses and trying to understand how people handle this in practice. Your example makes it clearer why the threshold needs to be specific to the strategy.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
The thing worth copying from practice is that nobody sets one number and leaves it there. The threshold gets set per strategy at the point the edge was measured, and it moves when the strategy is re-measured.

Is your tool watching the thesis inputs, or the realised fills against what the thesis assumed?

replies.author: Pupsi42069

replies.author: Pupsi42069
replies.body:
The comparison between programming and vibe coding should be analogous. Given your apt observation that a lot of “trash” is currently flooding the market, my comparison probably falls short. After all, in the context of trading, an ineffective approach is immediately invalid.

In my view, strategies will become obsolete because agent-based systems will make the right decisions based on the data provided—which is currently very accurate for some assets.

For example, I have a small team of agents controlling my browser for another topic. With the competition to develop the best and most affordable AI, it’s only a matter of time before the costs are low enough that the majority of people can run such agent systems. I’m not talking about 5–6 agents exchanging information with each other, but easily 2–3 times that number—if not more. And that's also the answer to your question. Validation is handled by a comprehensive agent system that can access all data 24/7 via a browser.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
“Core Theme Disrupted” example is the part I find really interesting.

Once you’ve defined the thesis and the drivers that would support or weaken it, how do you keep those conditions watched between your research sessions?

Do you already have something continuously monitoring those assumptions across earnings, market data, transcripts, etc., or is it mostly you + AI revisiting the thesis whenever new information arrives?

comments.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
comments.body:
Finding real alpha right now is extremely hard.  
Most people think the hard part is building the bot. It’s not. You can spin up a working system in a few days with current tools. The actual problem is that almost every simple edge on public price data is either already dead or too small to survive real costs and slippage.  
99% of newcomers assume the bot will “figure it out” for them. It won’t. The bot only executes whatever edge you managed to prove exists. If you didn’t do the ugly work of properly measuring costs, correcting for overlapping windows, multiple testing, and detection power — you’re just automating noise.  
The bottleneck was never the coding. It’s still the same as it always was: distinguishing a real, tradable edge from a pretty backtest.
